title: [BUG] "fix print on timesteps from file" errors when used alongside "dump on timesteps from file"
fix_hint: 变量互相引用。拆开定义顺序。

error_lines: Variable s2: has a circular dependency (src/variable.cpp:1148)
Fix print timestep variable returned a bad timestep: 0 (src/fix_print.cpp:170)
problem.text:
**Summary**

`fix print` errors when run on timesteps read through an equal-style variable from a file, if dumps are also being written on timesteps read through a (different) variable from a (different) file. Seems to go away if I comment out the equal-style variable _evaluation_ in `FixPrint::init()`.

**LAMMPS Version and Platform**

Ubuntu 24.04 on WSL2, LAMMPS release (11Feb 2026) or develop (patch_11Feb2026-263-g5c6749b73a)

**Expected Behavior**

The LAMMPS input:

```
variable f1 file timesteps1.txt
variable f2 file timesteps2.txt
variable s1 equal next(f1)
variable s2 equal next(f2)

dump 1 all atom 100 dump.lammpstrj
dump_modify 1 every v_s1 # with or without first yes
fix print all print v_s2 "$(step)"
```

should output `dump`s on every timestep in `timesteps1.txt` and `print` outputs on every timestep in `timesteps2.txt`.

**Actual Behavior**

Running the above snippet in `in.peptide` I get either:

```
ERROR: Variable s2: has a circular dependency (src/variable.cpp:1148)
```

or

```
ERROR: Fix print timestep variable returned a bad timestep: 0 (src/fix_print.cpp:170)
```

(line numbers from develop branch). This happens either on the second last line of `timesteps2.txt` or, if `timesteps2.txt` contains numbers larger than the total number of run steps, on the last "valid" print timestep in `timesteps2.txt`.

**Steps to Reproduce**

Add the above snippet to `in.peptide` before `run 300` and run the input. Sample timesteps1.txt:

```
4
10
30
60
80
100
200
500
```

Sample timesteps2.txt (errors with "circular dependency" on step 19):

```
5
12
19
204
```

Sample timesteps2.txt (identical to timesteps1.txt with added step 205, errors with "invalid timestep 0" on step 205):

```
4
10
30
60
80
100
200
205
500
```

**Further Information, Files, and Links**

in `fix_print.cpp` the timestep variable is evaluated during `init`:

```
 next_print = static_cast (input->variable->compute_equal(ivar_print));
 if (next_print ntimestep) error->all(FLERR, Error::NOLASTLINE,
 "Fix print timestep variable {} returned a bad timestep: {}", var_print,
 next_print);
```

Removing this evaluation is sufficient to restore expected behavior. Would be good to pin down the underlying bug.

Ideally we could add a `first yes` option to `fix print` similar to `dump_modify first yes`, as follows:

```
void FixPrint::init(){
 if (var_print) { ... // check ONLY var validity
 next_print = first_flag ? 0 : -1
 }
 modify->addstep_compute_all(next_print); // we need this, so next_print needs initializing
}

void FixPrint::setup(){
 end_of_step() // returns right away if next_print == -1
 if (next_print == -1) {
 next_print = evaluate_variable_and_error_if_invalid();
 }
}
```

This bug was discovered while trying to write this functionality for Matsci thread: https://matsci.org/t/any-issues-with-adding-a-first-option-to-fix-print/66954/4

solutions.author: akohlmey
solutions.text:
@srtee I think the problem is likely due to not having enough lines in both of the `timesteps?.txt` files. You need one more line than you want to output.
There is a very peculiar behavior of the `next()` function (or the "next" command) in that it will *delete* a file style variable when it has read the last line. Since the list of variables is compacted after a variable is deleted, the variable for those variables defined later (s1 and s2 in your case) will be decremented. So when the dump will try to evaluate the s2 variable, it uses an out-of-range index and the `Variable::compute_equal(int)` function returns 0 on evaluation of out of range variable indices. This would explain the invalid timestep error.
If you change the order how you define the equal and file style variables, you can end up using the index of the equal style variable that you are already evaluating instead of the file style variable you intend to read and that would explain the circular dependency error.

Correction: You need *two* more lines than used. Since you must have the last line being a timestep that you won't output anymore, you need one additional line so that file style variable is not deleted. Since you run for 300 steps, 500 is the last value to be read, but if that is the last value, the corresponding file style variable will already be deleted and since the file style variables must be defined before the equal style variables with the next() function, the equal style variables' index will already be shifted when one of the two file style variables is exhausted and thus deleted.

What worries me most about this is that the outcome is rather subtle and unexpected.

solutions.author: akohlmey
srtee
solutions.text:
Hi @akohlmey I am not sure that is what is happening here. (My original "replication script" would not have run because they used `v_f1` and `v_f2` -- I've changed them to `v_s1` and `v_s2` as they should be.)

In my experimenting, the `fix print` doesn't error when `dump` is running on a usual `every N` steps rather than on an equal-style variable. Also, I've set up my replication example to use two separate `next()` variables on two separate text files. I'll check whether the issue persists when adding more lines.

make a copy of the input and take the whole failing block out and make certain you have an input that works

then put things back in small pieces and run LAMMPS quickly after each addition

solutions.author: akohlmey
solutions.text:
dotdashdot:

ERROR: Variable zzlo: Invalid thermo keyword ‘i’ in variable formula (src/variable.cpp:2053)

Please look carefully at this error message. The error is not with the region command but with the definition of the variable it references.

 dotdashdot:

variable zzlo equal v_length*(i-1)
variable zzhi equal v_length*i

Both of these are incorrect. A variable is immediately expanded with ${name} and referenced in an expression with v_name. Your commands do neither and hence the error.

Besides, the whole process could be much simplified by using compute chunk/atom to set up a 1-d binning and compute reduce/chunk to get the stress per bin. No loop required.

solutions.author: akohlmey
solutions.text:
Oystein:

with 5632 atoms

This is a tiny number of atoms. GPUs cannot be efficient for this since there are not enough work units to run concurrently.

Please see LAMMPS Benchmarks for some (rather old) benchmark numbers comparing CPU and GPU performance. As you can see, you need to have a system that has two to three orders of magnitude more atoms to get significant speedup with a GPU versus a CPU. With current “Hopper” generation GPUs compared to the “Kepler” GPUs in the benchmark, the system size requirement to properly utilize the GPUs are even larger. Same for running across multiple GPUs.

solutions.author: akohlmey
solutions.text:
Oystein:

So I thought that perhaps still using several GPUs might speedup the ML model evaluation.

You can monitor the GPU utilization with the nvidia-smi command (you may need to request an interactive queue slot or log in a second time to the node running the job). Only if the GPU utilization is high, there is a chance to improve performance by using a second GPU.

You didn’t say which pair style you are using.

solutions.author: akohlmey
solutions.text:
Oystein:

Preliminary testing suggest that the scaling to several GPUs is not half bad

You should get even better performance, when compiling/using a GPU-aware MPI library.

Perhaps, it is worth notifying your HPC admins about that.

 Oystein:

This turned out to be a bit more involved than I thought.

This reminds me of a theorem formulated by my PhD adviser and a co-worker of his: the closer you look, the worse it gets.

title: [BUG] inconsistent results for fix addforce during minimization when using kokkos/cuda

error_lines: When using a single thread, the Kokkos Serial backend (i.e. Makefile.kokkos_mpi_only) gives better performance than the OpenMP backend (../kokkos.cpp:227)
Fixes cannot yet send exchange data in Kokkos communication, switching to classic exchange/border communication (../comm_kokkos.cpp:651)
problem.text:
**Summary**

Using `fix addforce` during `minimize` seems not to be working when using kokkos/cuda (`-k on g 1 -sf kk -pk kokkos`). Everything works as expected when using the same lammps binary with kokkos off.

**LAMMPS Version and Platform**

LAMMPS (8 Feb 2023) compiled with kokkos (Cuda,OpenMP)
gcc/8.3.1
cuda/11.2.0
IBM Power9 (lassen)

**Expected Behavior**

Here is a minimal input script that shows the issue. A perfect crystal with free surfaces along the z direction is created, then a stress of 100 MPa is applied to the free surface atoms using the `fix addforce` and the energy is minimized under this force:

```
units metal
atom_style atomic
boundary p p s

variable a0 equal 3.30263301805426
lattice bcc ${a0} orient x 1 1 1 orient y -1 2 -1 orient z -1 0 1
region box block 0 3 0 18 0 24 units lattice
create_box 1 box
create_atoms 1 box

change_box all triclinic

pair_style eam/alloy
pair_coeff * * newPP1_47-setfl.eam.alloy Ta
mass * 180.9479
neighbor 0.7 bin
neigh_modify every 1 delay 0

# Identify surface atoms
variable boundary_thickness equal 4.0
variable zlo0 equal "zlo+v_boundary_thickness"
variable zhi0 equal "zhi-v_boundary_thickness"
region upper block INF INF INF INF ${zhi0} INF units box
region lower block INF INF INF INF INF ${zlo0} units box
group upper region upper
group lower region lower
group surfaces union upper lower

# Identify central (bulk) atoms awy from the free surfaces
variable boundary_thickness equal 16.0
variable zlo0 equal "zlo+v_boundary_thickness"
variable zhi0 equal "zhi-v_boundary_thickness"
region bulk block INF INF INF INF ${zlo0} ${zhi0} units box
group bulk region bulk

compute 1 bulk pe/atom
compute ebulk bulk reduce sum c_1

compute 2 bulk stress/atom NULL virial
compute pbulk bulk reduce ave c_2[*]
variable Sxzmpa equal "0.1/0.5/v_a0^3*c_pbulk[5]"

thermo 100
thermo_style custom step pe c_ebulk v_Sxzmpa

# Apply shear tau (MPa)
variable tau equal 100.0
variable A equal "lx*ly"
variable energyConv equal 160217.662089
variable fx_upper equal "v_A/v_energyConv/count(upper)*v_tau"
variable fx_lower equal "-v_A/v_energyConv/count(lower)*v_tau"

fix 1 upper addforce ${fx_upper} 0.0 0.0
fix 2 lower addforce ${fx_lower} 0.0 0.0
fix_modify 1 energy yes
fix_modify 2 energy yes

minimize 0.0 1.0e-8 10000 10000
```

yes. they are. you must be resetting your temperature in some way,

which is the same as giving your system a kick. please check your

input. these data should be identical.

Also, could you explain more what do you mean by nature of MD causing

original and restarted runs to diverge? other than roundoff effects, I

suppose it includes convergence issues, but what else it may include?

it is not really roundoff, it is a truncation that happens when

you, e.g., add or subtract two numbers of different magnitude.

floating point math doesn't commute, so the result of sums

will depend on the order. a restart causes a neighbor list rebuild

and that will change the order in which properties like forces are

summed up which will make the trajectories diverge exponentially.

this is fundamental MD knowledge, check out in, e.g., the allen

and tildesley book.

unless you do fixed point math this will always happen. but this

is a small change and will manifest over time.

the convergence issue is independent. as the slide i was pointing

you to, you may think you have a converged result (the slide is

showing the first derivative(!) not the MSD, those look straight),

but you don't cover all modes in your system. a lot of mistakes

in MD analysis and thus differences in the published literature

happen because people don't know their time scales.
